--- title: "Introduction: the course and its toolkit" subtitle: "MLB7052.LT: Modern Methods in Molecular Ecology" title-slide-attributes: data-background-image: ../assets/logos/uu_sigill_right.png data-background-size: contain data-background-opacity: "0.25" author: "Peeter Laas" institute: "TalTech / UT Institute of Technology" format: revealjs: theme: [serif, ../css/lectures.scss] slide-number: false show-slide-number: all toc: true toc-depth: 1 progress: true width: 1200 height: 675 transition: slide toc-title: "Modern Methods in Molecular Ecology lecture:" smaller: true footer: "Fall 2026" logo: ../assets/logos/uu_sigill_right.png header-logo: ../assets/logos/UUtopleft.png self-contained: true code-line-numbers: true filters: - reveal-header execute: echo: true eval: false --- ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ```{=html} ``` --- ## General information | Field | Proposed specification | |---|---| | Course code | MLB7052.LT | | Course title | Kaasaegsed meetodid molekulaarses ökoloogias / Modern Molecular Methods in Ecology | | Semester | 2026/2027 autumn | | Language | Estonian teaching; English reading and software documentation | | Lecturer | Peeter Laas | | Assessment | Graded: A, B, C, D, E, F | | Intended audience | Advanced undergraduate and master's students in molecular ecology, biology, biotechnology, and related fields | ::: {style="margin-top:1em; font-size:0.78em; color:#777;"} Empty folder → 35 slides → shinyapps.io · 14.9°C in Tartu at render time ::: --- ## Course purpose ::: {.incremental} 1. understand the molecular principles behind DNA, RNA, proteins, genomes, gene expression, and molecular phenotypes; 2. understand the strengths, weaknesses, and appropriate uses of major molecular methods in ecology and evolutionary biology; 3. develop practical competence in sample design, nucleic-acid extraction, quantification, PCR, electrophoresis, sequencing, and basic computational analysis; 4. learn to connect molecular observations with ecological interactions, population structure, phylogeny, and environmental change; 5. develop reproducible habits for controls, contamination prevention, metadata, quality assessment, and scientific reporting; 6. design an end-to-end molecular study and defend the limitations of the proposed inference. ::: --- ## The main aim The course develops a working understanding of molecular biology and its use in ecological and evolutionary research. Students move from the molecular basis of information to a defensible study design: **biological question -> sample -> molecule -> assay -> sequence or measurement -> computation -> inference** ::: {.notes} The goal isn't to replace thinking — it's to reduce friction. You still need to understand the code. ::: --- # The course --- ## Course content {.scrollable} ::: {.dropdown-table}
Block I — Foundations and measurement - evolution, scientific reasoning, and molecular biology as a way of knowing; - chemical properties of DNA, RNA, proteins, buffers, enzymes, and molecular interactions; - information flow, replication, mutation, repair, recombination, transcription, translation, and regulation; - sample representativeness, preservation, extraction, quantification, inhibition, and contamination.
Block II — The molecular toolkit - electrophoresis, restriction analysis, Southern blotting, PCR, qPCR, ddPCR, Sanger sequencing, probes, FISH, fluorescence, and flow cytometry; - molecular markers, barcoding, metabarcoding, allozymes, RFLP, microsatellites, and SNPs; - Illumina, PacBio, Oxford Nanopore, library preparation, read quality, assembly, annotation, and data management.
Block III — Genomes and molecular phenotypes - comparative genomics, assembly, annotation, and public sequence databases; - transcriptomics, non-coding RNA, stage- and condition-specific regulation, epigenetics, and functional genomics; - proteomics, quantitative proteomics, protein interactions, post-translational modification, and molecular phenotypes; - the cell biology behind the traits we measure: life-cycle stages, secretion, transport, and cellular responses to the environment.
Block IV — Ecology, evolution, and application - phylogeny, phylogeography, population genetics, coalescence, and community-level inference; - species interactions, symbiosis, host-associated microbiota, and environmental monitoring; - CRISPR, LAMP, microfluidics, lab-on-chip, biosensing, and field-deployable diagnostics;
::: --- ## Contact [Mõned kasulikud raamatud](/drive.google.com/drive/folders/1O4cTmBxDmfk80coZbs7u1YtSVNmmd-Bt?usp=drive_link) ::: {.callout-important} email: peeter.laas@ut.ee; peeter.laas@taltech.ee; peeter.laas@gmail.com ::: Everything for the course — schedule, slides, seminar register, attendance — lives at [peeterlaas.github.io/MolEcoMeth](https://peeterlaas.github.io/MolEcoMeth/). --- ## Live data in slides — weather example Slides fetch real data at **render time**. No manual updates ever. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(httr2) resp <- request("https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast") |> req_url_query( latitude = 58.38, # Tartu longitude = 26.72, current = "temperature_2m,wind_speed_10m", timezone = "Europe/Tallinn" ) |> req_perform() |> resp_body_json() temp <- resp$current$temperature_2m wind <- resp$current$wind_speed_10m ``` ::: Then in slide text: ```markdown Temperature in Tartu right now: **14.9°C**, wind 15.5 km/h ``` **This title slide already does this** — look at the subtitle line. --- # Practical exercises --- ## Getting the dataset The EEA bathing water dataset (1990–2024) is **99 MB** — too large to embed in these slides. Scan to download: ::: {style="text-align:center;"} ![](/assets/photos/QRlink_to_driveshare.png){height=320px} `bw_assessment_eea_datahub_1990_2024_data.csv` 672,630 rows · 13 columns · all European bathing waters ::: --- ## Demo — downloadable table {.scrollable} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: --- ## Demo — interactive map ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: --- ## Exercise 1 — Explore the data (15 min) ```r library(readr) library(dplyr) bw <- read_csv("bw_assessment_eea_datahub_1990_2024_data.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) glimpse(bw) count(bw, countryCode, sort = TRUE) count(bw, quality) ``` Answer from the output, not from memory: - how many bathing waters does Estonia report, and over which years? - which quality categories exist, and how are they distributed? - which columns would you need to put a site on a map? --- ## Exercise 2 — Filter and summarise (15 min) ```r bw_ee <- bw |> filter(countryCode == "EE", season == 2024) bw_ee |> count(quality) |> mutate(share = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1)) |> arrange(desc(n)) ``` Then plot how the ratings have moved over time: ```r library(ggplot2) bw |> filter(countryCode == "EE") |> count(season, quality) |> ggplot(aes(season, n, fill = quality)) + geom_col(position = "fill") + labs(x = NULL, y = "share of sites", fill = NULL) ``` --- ## Exercise 3 — A searchable, downloadable table (15 min) A large data frame can be made browsable and downloadable: ```r library(DT) bw_ee |> select(bathingWaterName, bathingWaterType, lon, lat, quality, season) |> datatable( extensions = "Buttons", options = list( dom = "Bfrtip", buttons = c("csv", "excel"), pageLength = 15 ), filter = "top", # per-column filter boxes rownames = FALSE ) ``` This renders as an interactive HTML table with search, sort, and download — it works in any self-contained `.html` and in a Shiny app. --- ## Exercise 4 — Build the report (25 min) Put the three previous steps into one `report.qmd`: ```yaml --- title: "Estonian bathing waters, 1990-2024" format: html: toc: true embed-resources: true execute: echo: false --- ``` 1. read the data; 2. filter to Estonia; 3. show the searchable table; 4. plot the quality trend as a stacked bar chart; 5. `quarto render report.qmd`. The output is a single HTML file you can email, and the `.qmd` beside it says exactly how every number in it was produced. --- ## Key takeaways ::: {.incremental} - **`_quarto.yml`** = set your identity and style once, reuse forever - **Live data at render time** — slides and reports that never go stale - **`DT`** turns a 600,000-row table into something searchable and downloadable - **`leaflet`** puts sampling sites on a map in a dozen lines - **Self-contained HTML** travels as one file — no folder of assets to lose - **Commit first** — you cannot break what is already in git ::: --- ## Resources ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Learning:** - [quarto.org](https://quarto.org) — documentation and guides - [r4ds.hadley.nz](https://r4ds.hadley.nz) — R for Data Science - [open-meteo.com](https://open-meteo.com) — free weather API **R packages:** - `install.packages("DT")` - `install.packages("httr2")` - `install.packages("leaflet")` ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Data:** - [EEA Bathing Water Datahub](https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/datahub/datahubitem-view/3de879df-0935-4b2b-a69e-2571d09d5bc4) **Course site:** [peeterlaas.github.io/MolEcoMeth](https://peeterlaas.github.io/MolEcoMeth/) ![](/assets/photos/QRlink_to_driveshare.png){height=120px} ::: ::: --- ## Thank you {.center} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: {style="text-align:center; margin-top:1em;"} peeter.laas@ut.ee :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
